title: education, and: The poet imagines her ancestors watching her smoke a joint
abstract: education, and: The poet imagines her ancestors watching her smoke a joint Lark Omura (bio) education When the moon swells to gourdscan the shore for man o’war blue.If stung, use piss to calm. Green papaya also.It helps bee stings, has the same enzymesas meat tenderizer. Piss in the firepit campingwhen you wake and rise smelling country.Make sure it’s out before leaving.Never bury hot coals in the sand.Bury cowrie shells in the earth after soakingin fresh hosewater. Let the ants eat the meatout to avoid the smell. Dig up. If you smell funkdrifting from the rocks the fisherman probably hookeda reef shark by accident. Chain up the dog that day.Sharks have no bones. Sharks are not attracted to periodsbut watch out, someone’s been chumming the waterthere cause too many randos are parking by the gateto surf. The uncle who lives there will slash your tires.Sunday’s procession of lifted trucks is headingto the cockfights. Not a place for women but pregnant onesare good luck. Roosters help with centipedes.If you see a baby centipede its mother is likely near.If your mother needs help, show up.If you swallow a fishbone eat a ball of rice.Always soak your rice before cooking.Never take bananas on a boat. Never turn your backto the ocean. If you feel seasick, focus on land.When I die, scatter me from the rocksbehind the house. Let ’iwa birds circlingthe sky tell you when the rains will come. [End Page 163] The poet imagines her ancestors watching her smoke a joint from the pearl cloud distance they observe herunending frequencies of light multiply watch with fascination this girl with the short brown hair fold dry leaf into paper and twist tip of her tongue sliding across an edge scattered contents of her desk, her deliberateness. they exchange an amused nod downward at her small expertise performance of ritual still, she is captivating. fingertips courting an opal flamecheeks tense with inhale as thin gray threads of smoke unfold, an ancient dance beckoning not an intentional offering, yet they choose to interpret it as such here in the chambers of forever everything is motion dissolving study the bone curve of her nose, hairline her flickering eyes, maps leading back to themselves [End Page 164] how she gazes unknowingly down the endless hall stares directly at them thinking she is watching sheets of raindrops slant toward earth mostly they sit fascinated with her young beautyfollow the arc of her pupils out the window to the yellow-flower yard in her apartment five talismans glow among the earthly clutter: brass incense stand and candle holder clear glass beads strung on purple rope with tassels bolt of indigo shibori fabric purple silk kimono carefully wrapped in a trash bag and folded into a plastic bin they smile. both women loved purple and salty dried foods simple pleasures of being human the title of her latest poem makes them inhale softly at the word she uses to describe them: ancestors they were so young once. two soft bodies walking over this spinning, tree-covered thing [End Page 165] even from above there is no articulating its wonder the tip of the joint brightens orange, then disappears into the black hole of its burning gut, smoke replaces solid nothing where something once stood, choosingits colors in a mirror. the eternal clarity of beauty and pain two stones marking an entrance. [End Page 166] Lark Omura Lark Omura was born and raised on the island of Maui and currently lives in Brooklyn. She is a vona and Winter Tangerine workshop alum and was received a Hillary Gravendyk memorial scholarship from the Community of Writers at Squaw Valley. Her poetry has been published in the Offing, Aster(ix), Bamboo Ridge, and the Hawaii Review, among other places. She is currently an mfa candidate in poetry at Rutgers University–Newark. title: Postcards
abstract: Postcards Jeremy Brewster, Glenna Sloan, Michelle Gonzalez, Ines Galling, Claudia Soeffner, Tanja Nathanael, Tilka Jamnik, and Alicia Muñoz Alvarez Children’s rhymes from twenty-two different countries are presented in this unique contribution to international children’s literature. The rhymes are written in the original language (including Chinese, norwegian, Hindi, Shona, Arabic, and Danish) as well as in English. Included are chants, bits of longer poems and ballads, and short rhymes about themes important to young children such as eating, sleeping, singing, playing, and exploring the natural world. Clearly evident in all the selections are the strong rhythms and satisfying refrains of these poems. Mique Moriuchi has used richly textured paint and collage techniques to create the double-spread backgrounds. The animals and natural settings are brightly portrayed and invite close inspection. While it is understood that such an undertaking can only include some of the world’s languages, I found it quite disappointing there was not an entry from a Spanish-speaking country, especially when one considers the huge number of Spanish speakers in the world. Jeffrey Brewster Danielle Wright, collector. My Village: Rhymes from Around the World Illus. Mique Moriuchi Wellington, New Zealand: Gecko Press, 2008. London: Frances Lincoln Children’s Books, 2010. 53 pp. ISBN: 9781847800862 (poetry collection, 4 – 10) [End Page 8] Readers young and old will find much to admire in this strikingly beautiful book that combines fine art, poetry, musical score, and history. Folk singer Lightfoot’ s song eloquently de scribes the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, “An iron road runnin’ from the sea to the sea.“ “Canadian Railroad Trilogy,” commissioned by t he CBC in 1967 for Canada ’s centennial year, is a node to Canada’ s natural beauty, a passion ate report of a technological feat that changed the country, and a celebration of those who toiled and sacrificed to make the railroad possible. Modeled on another song, “Civil War Trilogy” by Bob Gibson, the book includes the music and the lyrics, notes on the magnificent pastel drawings by award- winning artist Ian Wallace, a brie f history of t he railroad, and suggestions for further reading. Lightfoot, Canada ’ s most famous folksinger, son g writer, and guitarist is, among other honors, a member of the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame. Glenna Sloan Gordon Lightfoot Canadian Railroad Trilogy Illus. Ian Wallace Toronto, Canada: Groundwood, 2010. 56 pp. ISBN: 9780888999535 (picture book, all ages) [End Page 32] Time in all its varied shapes and forms is the theme of this collection of poetry. The days of the week go on holiday, the months of the year are personified, and the uniqueness of each season is wittily described. How does time feel when you are waiting for someone special? For norac, waiting can feel so long that “a toad can turn into a prince three times over” and “the millipedes have time to tie their shoes.” For children, time takes on new meaning when on a holiday. Routines are broken and fantasies explored. norac effectively uses rhythm to de scribe the se occasions, such as when imitating the bouncing of a ball or the excitement of a Carnival celebration. The colored pencil illustrations add much to the surreal imagery of the language. Crowther’s subdued tones come alive with expressive eyes and insects conversing. Some poems even come with delightful instructions, such as “to be recited under the sun with a chorus of insects” or “to be whispered at bedtime on a snowy night.” Here are forty poems to be read over time and time again. Michelle Gonzalez Carl Norac Petits poèmes pour passer le temps (Short Poems to Pass the Time) Illus. Kitty Crowther Paris, France: Didier Jeunesse, 2008. 57pp. ISBN: 978-2-278-06183-9 (poetry, 6 and up) [End Page 38] Philosophical, playful, funny, and melancholy – that’s how you could describe the poems of Hans Christian Andersen Awardwinning author Jurg Schubiger. The verses in It’s the Wind’s Birthday are both light-hearted and meaningful. They often veer off the road to make readers pause, smile, ponder, and then read the poem a second, third, or even fourth time. Both children and adults can easily identify...

title: Voices from Kibuli Country by Dannabang Kuwabong
abstract: Reviewed by: Voices from Kibuli Country by Dannabang Kuwabong Sharif El Gammal-Ortiz (bio) Kuwabong, Dannabang. Voices from Kibuli Country. Toronto: TSAR, 2013. An order where we can at last grow up to that which we stored up as we grew. An order which satisfies all that is appetitive in the intelligence and prehensile in the affections. —Seamus Heaney, “Crediting Poetry” “For scars are not evil but stories of conquest of evil” (48). That line, from the twenty-fourth poem of Voices from Kibuli Country, proclaims not only the speaker’s desire to strike a [End Page 218] balance between the numinous energies carrying him through Ghana, Canada, the United States, Puerto Rico, St. Martin, St. Croix, and Dominica (just to name a few), but also his innate sensibility to create the head-to-heart space where all his voices can converge in one outstanding celebratory hymn. Dannabang Kuwabong divides the collection, his fifth publication of creative writing and fourth book of poems, into two parts: “Those Who Step into Shadows” and “Massacre,” respectively. The first part, sixteen poems in length, and the second, a much heftier thirty-three, combine together for a grand total of forty-nine poems. The reader gets the feeling, as the collection moves from all the way up north in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada; through the United States in Athens, Ohio, and Charlotte, North Carolina; then down towards Haiti veering further southeast to San Juan, Puerto Rico; on downwards still to St. Croix and further east to the island of St. Martin; and in a powerful thrust heading southwards towards Dominica, to finally land in a place more spiritual than geographical with the two great “Joan Fayer” poems, that Kuwabong’s project is one of concatenating the associative links celebrating, again, the ontological oneness of Being. The twenty-third and twenty-fourth poems, with the long titles of “While listening to Dr. Jack Coulehan read poems about his patients” and “Watching slides of scars while Jim Ferris performs a poem about scars,” give the reader glimpses into Kuwabong’s psychic centers while presenting memorable characters like the six hundred pound man and the Sankofa bird tangentially as well as imagery which is as powerfully organic as it is subtle. From the “Dr. Coulehan” poem, let’s hear: So you see, my six-hundred pounds Jamaican brother dying in America We may be heartbroken at your rapture but we are heart-emboldened To know that the Sankofa bird has carried you above raging waters To where you can tell your stories of migration to those to come In the nine-nights of our memory where you ride those with vision And give us strength each year on ancestral remembrances days Across this island of hopes deferred yet reborn in your passing (46) The strangeness of this pained, morbidly obese man, his bodily prison as it metaphors the Middle Passage, in turn juxtaposed to the Sankofa bird of the Ghanaian Akan language meaning to reach back and get to it, works in that it is in keeping with the axiom: no wrong comes from remembering the forgotten. And the organically powerful imagery of “Watching slides of scars”—its sixty-fourth line the opening of this review—has the speaker reflecting on the genesis of his title poem. Let’s listen: So my title poem will begin with a grated knee My poem will echo the sound from a cleft on the hunches My poem will be a shadow of a dry river of blood Overhanging the knee cap protruding like a swollen testicle My poem will be a hanging membrane like an unwanted earlobe (47) to [End Page 219] My poem will be a scar against poetry Blobs of unfinished flesh rising like dough Like a cowboy in a bandit’s sombrero (47) and finally to the poetic voice equating the scar on his left arm to “a poem yet to be read / It is an aesthetic of a veritable millipede slapped stuck” (48). Notice how the grotesque imagery in distorting the reader’s perception quickly snaps it shut, so that, in remaining closed, it soon takes on a settling effect. title: Monoblemma sheari Martínez, 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Monoblemma sheari sp. nov. Figures 1–3. Type material. Holotype: VENEZUELA. Sucre: 15 km W of Carupano, Thorn-scrub ravine soil washing, 50 m, [10°39′54.72″N, 63°23′27.66″W], S. and J. Peck leg., 29.VIII.1987, 1 ♂ (AMNH _ IZC 00480924). Paratypes: same data as the holotype, 1 ♀♀ (AMNH _ IZC 00480923), 4 ♀♀ (AMNH _ IZC 00480914); same data but 80 m, 2 ♀♀ (AMNH _ IZC 00480913). Etymology. The specific epithet is a patronym honoring William Shear, pioneer in the study of the Tetrablemmidae and a major contributor to the knowledge of the opiliofauna and millipede fauna of North America, whose work has inspired new generations of researchers. Diagnosis. Monoblemma sheari sp. nov. is similar to Monoblemma becki Brignoli, 1978 in the absence of eyes (Fig. 3C–D), but it can be distinguished from this species and from the remaining congeners by the laminar, short, and distally expanded embolus, and by the spermatic duct with a wide lumen in its distal section (Figs. 2A–D, 3A). Females differ from the known females of the genus by having smaller receptacles, thinner copulatory ducts, and a shorter central process (Figs. 2E–F, 3B). Description. Male (holotype, AMNH_IZC 00480924). Total body length 1.57, carapace length 0.78, width 0.57, height 0.34. Sternum sub-rhomboidal with recurved posterior edge, length 0.42, width 0.41. Chelicerae (paturon) length 0.22. Legs: Leg I—femur 0.44/ patella 0.17/ tibia 0.30/ metatarsus 0.20/ tarsus 0.24/ total 1.37; II—0.40/ 0.13/ 0.26/ 0.18/ 0.23/ 1.22; III—0.34/ 0.11/ 0.24/ 0.15/ 0.19/ 1.06; IV—0.36/ 0.13/ 0.26/ 0.24/ 0.26/ 1.27. Abdomen length 0.85, width 0.66. Body coloration pale orange, with the carapace slightly darker (Fig. 1A–C). Legs orange, with whitish to light-brown patches. Spinnerets pale yellow. Carapace. with reticulate cephalic region, with small granules along the borders, suboval, the anterior margin strongly projected; without eyes, clypeus not clearly defined (Fig. 1A–C). Chelicerae oblique, bearing a very small frontal apophysis, anteriorly positioned (Figs. 1B–C, 2C). Endites with the internal section subquadrangular and anteriorly projected. Labium trapezoidal and wider than long. Sternum rugose, almost as long as wide (Fig. 1C). Legs. Legs bearing fine setae; femora with granulated cuticle; tibiae and tarsi with striated cuticle; tarsi longer than metatarsi. Abdomen. With fine white setae on the posterior edge (Fig. 1A); dorsal scutum oval and smooth; ventral (pulmonary) scutum finely reticulated and bearing fine setae (Fig. 1A); four lateral scuta present, extending to the posterior margin of the anal plate; lateral regions with thin free sclerites (Fig. 1B); postgenital scutum narrow and rectangular; preanal scutum rectangular, approximately as wide as the pulmonary scutum, with straight lateral edges. Palp. Femur cylindrical and slightly swollen, with simple setae; patella short, bearing short setae; tibia swollen, with simple and long setae; cymbium very narrow, covered with long setae on the apical side. Bulb large, pyriform; spermatic duct very wide at the base, narrowing toward the embolus, with a medial expansion and a distal section with a wide lumen. Embolus short (less than half the bulb length), laminar, and apically subquadrangular (Figs. 1A–D, 2A). Female (paratype, AMNH_IZC 00480923). Total body length 1.73, carapace length 0.73, width 0.59, height 0.35. Sternum length 0.45, width 0.45. Chelicerae (paturon) length 0.18. Legs: Leg I—femur 0.41/ patella 0.17/ tibia 0.31/ metatarsus 0.22/ tarsus 0.27/ total 1.40; II—0.41/ 0.15/ 0.27/ 0.21/ 0.24/ 1.30; III—0.35/ 0.14/ 0.18/ 0.18/ 0.22/ 1.10; IV— 0.35/ 0.16/ 0.35/ 0.25/ 0.29/ 1.42. Abdomen length 1.03, width 0.83. Coloration as in the male; legs orange with whitish to light-brown patches (Fig. 2D–F). Carapace with smooth cephalic region, with posterior striation; anterior margin projected (Fig. 2D), thoracic region rugose (Figs. 2D, 3D). Chelicerae with small frontal apophyses (Fig. 3D). Endites subquadrangular, with a wide basal edge narrowing toward the distal edge (Fig. 2F). Labium trapezoidal and wider than long (Fig. 2F). Sternum rugose, with few setae along the margins (Fig. 2F). Abdomen. Covered with fine white setae (Figs. 2D, 3D). Scuta as in the male; postgenital scutum narrower. Genitalia. Genital orifice small, located at the posterior margin of the epigynal fold. Central process thin and distally rounded. Seminal receptacles small, irregular in shape but appearing subrounded when immersed in alcohol, membranous; vulval ducts short and thin (Figs. 2E–F, 3B). Variation. Females (n=5): total length: 1.67–1.73; carapace length: 0.69–0.73. In some females, the coloration is paler. Distribution. Only known from Venezuela (Fig. 4). Note. The new species Monoblemma sheari sp. nov. exhibits a median expansion in the spermatic duct of the bulb, a feature shared with other members of the genus and most pronounced in Monoblemma cubaense Martínez, 2025, and Monoblemma cambridgei (Bryant, 1940). However, the laminar embolus and the other characters mentioned in the diagnosis section are unique to this species. Monoblemma unicum Gertsch, 1941 Monoblemma unica Gertsch, 1941: 10, figs. 9–12 (male holotype from Barro Colorado Island, Canal Zone, Panama, 9.VI.1938 E. G. Williams, Jr. leg., deposited in AMNH, examined). Monoblemma unicum Shear, 1978: 21, figs. 47–50 (correction of specific epithet according to the gender of the generic name); Nentwig, 1993: 97, figs. 48A–C. Monoblemma unicum Martínez, 2025: 289, figs. 1A–C, E–I, 20C. Additional material examined. Dominican Republic. Pedemales: 24 km N of Cabo Rojo, wet forest, litter near termite mound, 610 m, [18°07′01″N, 71°38′46″W], M.A. Ivie, T. K. Philips & K.A. Johnson leg., 20.VIII.1988, 1 ♂ (USNMENT 02180844). Note. The additional specimen examined herein presents a reddish coloration, although the male palp morphology and the position of the single eye are consistent with the holotype. Distribution. Known from Panama and Dominican Republic (Fig. 4).

title: Scars
abstract: Margaret Edwards Margaret Edwards was born and brought up in Atlanta, Georgia. She earned her B.A. at Bryn Mawr, and her M.A. and Ph.D. at Stanford. She now teaches creative writing and American poetry at the University of Vermont, Burlington. Having studied poetry writing at Stanford under Donald Davie, she turned to fiction ten years ago and has stayed primarily with that form. Her stories have appeared in The Virginia Quarterly Review, The Greensboro Review, The Mississippi Review, Redbook, Gallimaufry, and Tri-Quarterly. She has recently completed a novella and has plans for a novel. Scars HIS DOG HAD bitten a child. It was very late in the afternoon when Ted Landy stepped into the kitchen, closed the back door, and took off his gloves. "I've seen the boy," he said. "It doesn't look good." His wife, Joann, was setting the kitchen table for a light supper. She was dressed in a long plaid skirt, a jersey turtleneck and a strand of pearls. "You're going with the girls?" He hadn't expected that. "I thought we said we'd let them go alone this year," he said. "I want to go. It will help me keep my mind off what happened. I should think you'd want some distraction too." She was setting the four places. Ted sat down in his usual chair and watched her align the knife, fork and spoon in front of him. "Well, what about the boy?" Joann did not stop moving, but her voice had the enforced quiet tone, the determined lilt, of anxiety. "It's bad. Very bad. He got bit all right. Lovejoy did a real job on him." "Oh, Ted!" Joann had pulled the paper napkins out of the dispenser. Now she stood holding them. "How bad? You actually saw him?" "Like this." With his finger on his own face Ted drew a line from the middle of his right eyebrow over the bridge of his nose, then another line from the right corner of his mouth into the center of his cheek. The red lines in the boy's face had been sewn with black thread, two angry centipedes. "Over fifty stitches." Joann shook her head. "And he's only eight - in the girls' grade at school. What possessed Lovejoy?" Lovejoy was their Doberman pinscher. He had been a gift to Ted from a friend who owed him money. "Champion stock. Doesn't look like five hundred dollars yet, but he will," said the friend, depositing the wriggling black puppy on the floor where he began to frolic, skidding on the linoleum. Joann had named him. Lovejoy outgrew his name as he began to fulfill the friend's prediction. He became a sleek five-hundreddollar 's worth and loped along the streets of the small Vermont town looking as aggressive, errant, prosperous and acquisitive as a ski tourist. He roamed. He snapped. They had to keep him penned. He loved the family exclusively and threw himself against the cyclone fence at strangers with a ferocity that had, at one time, pleased Ted. That something so elegant and dark and temperamental was protecting him made Ted feel secretly happy, though he protested to friends that he would "do something" about Lovejoy's bad manners. He hung a Beware Dog sign near the garage - "where no one could see it," Joann had pointed out - but he had hung it. It had really never occurred to him that Margaret Edwards The Missouri Review ¦ 207 Lovejoy's threats were real. He thought Lovejoy troublesome, annoying, loud, rude - yet never dangerous. Joann placed a folded paper napkin by his fork. She turned to the stove and began to serve the plates. "The girls have been crying and sitting on the stairs hugging him ever since they got home. title: The deceitfulness of beetles
venue: Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment
abstract: A legend from southern Africa, recounted by James A Honey in his 1910 book South-African folk-tales, tells of how the ants – tired of being the prey of aardvarks, birds, centipedes, and the like – held a great council to discuss how to build a more secure type of home that would suit them all. No consensus was reached, however, and the ants continued to construct their various types of shelter, each kind in its own way. Upon hearing of their discord, the Insect King decided to send them the secret of unity, and a message: work together. He chose Beetle as his envoy, but this courier never made it to the ants, and that is why today they still have so many types of nest. But is this the real reason for their diversity? There is evidence that Beetle did not lose his way at more sinister agenda. Ants of different species may not be good at working together, but within their own colonies they can be among the most organized and disciplined of all living things. Workers, soldiers, and queens unrelentingly perform their separate tasks, all pulling together seamlessly as one grand superorganism. Such organization requires communication, and we have long known that ants converse via touch and chemical cues. It is, however, becoming increasingly clear that they also communicate acoustically. Several species are now known to rub their legs against bristles on their abdomens to make sounds, an act known as stridulation. The black fire ant Solenopsis richteri, for example, stridulates differently to signal distress versus alarm. Leaf-cutter ants of the species Atta caphaloes stridulate to tell their comrades when they are prevented from moving freely. And the queens and pupae of different Myrmica species use stridulation to “speak” with the workers who attend them. But no ants stridulate as strenuously as Matabele ants (Pachycondyla analis [synonym Megaponera foetens]). Matabele ants on the march. It was on a moonlit night in the Limpopo Province of South Africa when I first heard them. During an anti-poaching patrol, the headlights of our vehicle lit up a black band, some 20 cm across, moving with visible purpose across the track ahead of us. Our ranger guide stopped and told us to place our ears close to the moving Matabele mass (although not too close lest we receive a very painful bite), and to listen. In the silence, the little black army, on its way to raid a termite nest (for this is what Matabele ants do), made a constant fizzing sound like an open bottle of soda. Perhaps, I thought, their stridulations helped them maintain their tight, military formation. Blowing gently on them increased the volume of their fizzing – their announcement of alarm – but it did not halt them, and within a minute they had disappeared on their way to assault their chosen victims. On the 25th of March 1914, at a meeting of the Rhodesia Scientific Association, G Arnold, curator of the Rhodesia Museum, gave an account of his own, extraordinary encounter with these sonorous creatures, and of the social parasites that accompanied them as they changed their nest site (Proc Rhodesia Sci Assoc 1914; XIII: 25–32). His words bring much uncertainty to Honey's old folk tale. “Looking down [the ants'] hole, [various] guests and parasites could be seen climbing up the walls in an almost continuous stream, hastening to join their hosts in their new home. These insects comprised a Lepisma, two species of staphylinid beetles, a histerid beetle and an onthophagous beetle; there was also a spider. The Lepismas as usual were very plentiful; of the larger staphylinid I saw only one specimen, but of the smaller sort and of the other beetles very many examples occurred... This motley crew of cringers, thieves, murderers and body-snatchers did not appear to attract the slightest attention from their victims the ants, which were too busy with the work in hand to waste any time on the rabble following in their wake.” Arnold's account suggests that the Insect King's courier did indeed reach the ants, but finding sustenance aplenty among their larders and their brood, decided not to deliver the message with which he was charged. And there he has stayed until this day. But how does he trick the ants into not attacking him? The caterpillars of Maculinea butterflies, which parasitize Myrmica ant nests, might hold the answer: they not only produce the same chemical signals as their hosts, but also make the same sounds, and thus receive care and attention rather than being thrown out. Some staphylinid, histerid, and scarabeid beetles are also thought to stridulate. Perhaps, then, Beetle remains unnoticed because he says the right things. If only the Insect King had known of Beetle's potential for deceit! Had he sent someone else, what wonderful, secure homes might all ants now have?

title: Planet Soil
abstract: Verkerk, M (Director). (2023). Planet Soil: The Power of the Underground. Collective Eye Films. 83 mins. Planet Soil is a Dutch documentary directed by Mark Verkerk that makes the case for understanding soil not as inert ground beneath our feet but as a teeming, interdependent living system fundamental to food security, climate stability, and ecological health. Combining groundbreaking microscopy, time-lapse photography, animation, and macro videography with accessible storytelling, the film is able to engage school-age viewers with enough substantive content to fascinate undergraduate students in introductory biology or environmental science courses. The film is structured around a series of sites and practitioners in the Netherlands. These include the regenerative strip farm of Folkert Botma in Engwierum, Friesland; a farm in Abcoude in the Province of Utrecht; Wouter van Eck’s food forest at Kettleburg; Tuin van Brasa in Amsterdam Zuidoost, a community park and garden built over a freeway tunnel; and the living rooftop gardens atop some 300 bus stops across the city of Utrecht, where researchers are mapping fungal biodiversity across an urban landscape. Together these sites build a cumulative argument that soil health is urgent and relevant in cities as well as on farms. The film introduces a substantial cast of scientists and researchers whose work anchors its scientific claims. Pier Oosterkamp explains the mechanical structure of healthy soil and how microbial activity creates the formations that allow air and water circulation. Soil biologists Ingrid Lubbers and Jan Willem Groenigen of Wageningen University conduct worm surveys that illustrate how earthworm diversity signals broader soil health. At AMOLF, the Institute for Atomic and Molecular Physics in Amsterdam, Professor Toby Kiers and researcher Loreto Oyarte Galvez demonstrate an imaging robot capable of capturing high-resolution, real-time images of fungal networks across forty plates simultaneously. Their invention allows researchers to track carbon and nutrient flow between plant roots and competing fungal networks. Toby Kiers describes these exchanges in terms of supply, demand, and trading strategies that function like a biological market. The film also documents research using DNA technology to measure microbial diversity across fifty different farms, revealing that strip-farmed soils (the soil preservation and sustainability technique described by Farmer Folkert Botma) harbor more than 9,000 species of protozoa compared to roughly 2,000 in soils heavily treated with pesticides and artificial fertilizer. This abundance of microscopic sold life is directly connected to crop health and reduced pesticide dependency. The film introduces a category labeled “soil animals” which encompasses organisms across a vast range of scales. On-screen labels identify species by both common and scientific names and append size measurements in millimeters or fractions thereof, allowing viewers to develop a concrete spatial imagination of the soil food web. A snail, a fly larva, a mite, and a nematode are labeled and scaled in this way; and a tardigrade (water bear) appears at 0.5mm. The film also presents the well-supported claim that 75% of all terrestrial carbon is stored in below-ground systems, positioning healthy soil as a major and underappreciated lever in climate change mitigation. Visually, Planet Soil represents a genuine achievement in cinematography. Microscopy sequences reveal soil aggregates, fungal hyphae (the long branching filaments that make up the majority of fungal bodies) and nematode locomotion at extraordinary magnification; time-lapse photography captures decay, fungal and mushroom growth, and mycelium development with beauty. The film repeatedly opens windows onto truly beautiful worlds invisible to the naked eye while never losing sight of the familiar creatures, snails, bees, worms, and moles, that share the same subterranean ecosystem. Verkerk’s allows extended passages run without narration or dialogue, trusting the imagery alone to carry the argument. These wordless sequences invite the viewer to observe and absorb rather than be instructed, and they speak to a filmmaker confident in the appeal of his material. The film’s structural rhythm reinforces this approach between the finely focused and the larger human (and ecological) systems. Verkerk moves fluidly between the microscopic world and the human-scale world, between the laboratory and the community garden, between the individual organism and the soil ecology. Scenes of children handling millipedes and peering through microscopes at nematodes from their own garden soil capture the moment when, as the film puts it, fear gives way to wonder. The cardboard sheet-mulching method demonstrated early in the film is one of several concrete, replicable techniques that give the film practical utility beyond its scientific content. Verkerk grounds scientific ideas in human narratives. Tuin van Brasa, is a community garden built over a freeway tunnel which connects previously divided neighborhoods in Amsterdam Zuidoost. The park and garden broadens the film’s scope to encompass urban social connections as well as ecological regeneration. The film closes on a quotation from pioneering American soil scientist Charles E. Kellogg: “Essentially, all life depends upon the soil ... There can be no life without soil and no soil without life; they have evolved together.” This idea crystallizes the film’s central argument linking the co-evolution of soil and life. The film’s one notable limitation is its geographic concentration: all sites in the Netherlands. While the scientific principles are universal, the film largely sets aside the economic, political, policy related and structural barriers that farmers in other contexts would face in adopting regenerative methods. That said, it would have been encouraging to see some evidence or statistical information about the adoption of regenerative methods in other nations or regions of the worlds. Educators using the film with advanced students may wish to supplement it with comparative materials addressing these challenges in different agricultural and socioeconomic settings. Planet Soil is a well-crafted documentary that succeeds on multiple levels. It functions as an introduction to soil biology for general and younger audiences, as a primer on regenerative agriculture for educators and practitioners, and as a visually and scientifically rich resource for undergraduate courses in ecology, environmental science, or sustainable agriculture. Its argument that soil health, food security, climate resilience, and community well-being are inseparable, is made with evidence, warmth, filmmaking skill. Awards: Winner, New York SCIENCE & NATURE FEEDBACK Film & Screenplay Festival

title: The Prodigious Pustule
Inside Appalachia
abstract: The pleasure of listening to Inside Appalachia is that of visiting an old friend with whom you assuredly slip back into the same ongoing conversation each time you reconnect. Small talk is unnecessary, and so much that is already understood need not be said. The acclaimed radio show is hosted weekly by Mason Adams and broadcast through stations affiliated with West Virginia Public Broadcasting. Previous episodes are also available as podcasts via multiple platforms. While the show's mission is to highlight the cultural heritage of West Virginia and the region, its geographic and topical scope is as broad and far-reaching as Appalachia itself. Tuning in or listening to an episode as a podcast, you are reminded of the days before cable television was extended out to the rural routes, and you sat transfixed each Sunday morning as Charles Kuralt's reassuring and incomparable voice led you on a wide-ranging journey for the curious mind. On any given week, you might learn something new about art or music or history or politics or food or anything else. And somehow, all of it is connected, all of it offered in a way that is both accessible and refined. Inside Appalachia is the kind of show that presumes a roving kind of inquisitiveness on the part of its audience.More importantly, Inside Appalachia bids listeners to know the region as a place that comes into our consciousness in the interwoven, complex, and dynamic elements of the natural environment, the built environment, and the range of human stories and cultures that exist here. This stands in stark contrast to the often reductive, one-dimensional profiles offered by other media coverage that tend to rely on Appalachia as the stand-in of choice for any of an array of social and political ailments—or, equally vexing, programs that cleave to the same tired, nostalgic, and romanticized notions of homogenous rural or working-class ideologies. Inside Appalachia offers a portrait of the region that is unsentimental, but that is nevertheless shaped and created with care and affection.Given the show's history—it has been on the air for over twenty years now—Inside Appalachia should be considered remarkable for the way it continues to avoid encapsulating the region into a few overused themes. Certainly, you might encounter here and there a story about Dolly Parton or moonshine, but the content is generally ever shifting and vital. There is always something new to consider. In this way, it is a reminder of the character Carrie Bishop's viewpoint in the novel Storming Heaven (1987) by Denise Giardina: “There is enough to study in these hills to last a lifetime” (89).The lineup of episodes over the last half or so of 2022 spanned the widest imaginable reach of topics, issues, and subjects, from millipedes to maternal health care, to a butchering apprenticeship program, and most things in-between. Listening to but a handful of shows, you come away thinking that every corner and fold of this landscape offers something else to know and ponder. Like taking an audio road trip through the heart of the region, you regularly come across unusual or little-known places such as Cuz's Uptown Barbecue in Pounding Mill, Virginia. Yet the show proffers far more than curiosities and feel-good stories.Inside Appalachia tackles the most pressing and factious questions facing the region, including those related to the opioid epidemic, and the now commonplace devastating floods born of environmental degradation, which have impacted communities throughout the mountains. While the marker of the show is that episodes are mostly narrated through the stories of ordinary people who live here and who call the mountains home, the program also offers listeners the opportunity to hear from widely recognized authors like Silas House, Barbara Kingsolver, and Beth Macy. At the same time, in an understanding of the region as a place that is continually evolving and being reshaped, Inside Appalachia covers fresh thinking and viewpoints. Two highlights that capped off the 2022 season were interviews with Z. Zane McNeill, editor of a newly published collection of writing from queer voices in the region, Y'all Means All: The Emerging Voices Queering Appalachia (2022), and with West Virginia's state folklorist, Emily Hilliard, whose new book Making Our Future: Visionary Folklore and Everyday Culture in Appalachia (2022) presents folklife in Appalachia through visionary and dynamic forms of cultural expression.Of note as well are ongoing conversations around particular issues. Throughout the summer, multiple episodes presented portions of a series that explored economic, moral, and social questions around dog racing. Beyond Inside Appalachia, it may not have otherwise been possible to know that West Virginia is now the only state where tracks used for the problematic sport of greyhound racing can still be found. It is illegal nearly everywhere else in the country. And, long after the catastrophic flooding in eastern Kentucky in late July had become buried in the national news cycle, the show continued to revisit families and communities as they tried to piece their lives back together there. The extended coverage of such issues on the show help to frame the region as multidimensional and interconnected rather than as a static, monolithic culture.Finally, for longtime fans of Inside Appalachia, a retrospective episode that aired in August and that celebrates twenty years of the show is one not to be missed. It features a conversation with founders Giles Snyder and Beth Vorhees as they look back in celebration and discuss the early days of the program. For those just discovering Inside Appalachia, that episode serves to introduce a new generation of listeners to its distinct vision to delve into all the complex layers of a region that offers a lifetime (and more) of contemplation.

title: Interaction of the fluctuation of the population density of sweet potato pests with changes in farming practices, climate and physical environments: A 11-year preliminary observation from South-Kivu Province, Eastern DRCongo
abstract: Sweetpotato is a major food security crop grown in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Its production is however limited due to high prevalence of pests and diseases among other abiotic and biotic factors. A study was designed to aid understanding the knowledge of farmers about pests and their perception about climate variability impacts, as well as documenting the phenology of sweetpotato pests (pest population dynamics) in relationship with weather factors. The paper aimed at determined which climatic factors may be used as best predictors of the different status of pest populations (declines, outbreaks). Farmer based data was obtained using a semi structured questionnaire administered to several of farmers. Population dynamics of sweetpotato pests were monitored year-round from 2005 to 2015 in South Kivu province, eastern DRCongo. Field monitoring (visual counts) observations (population dynamic of different soil-dwelling and surface dwelling arthropods visiting sweetpotato fields) combined with a survey of farmers’ knowledge on sweetpotato pests and their practices in the management of these pests in South- Kivu Province were conducted for 11 years. Monitoring (with field observations and counts) was carried out in fields under different farming practices (monocropping and inter-cropping) in sites located at different altitudes. Similarly, data for climatic factors, for the same period, were collected from Lwiro Research center. Regression models were applied to understand the linkages between environmental factors (rainfall and temperature) and pest population dynamics. The results indicated that different varieties (local and improved ones) of sweetpotato are grown three times (3 seasons) per annum under various cropping systems (sole crop, mixed crops) in various agroecological zones at different altitudes. Various arthropod species visit the crop at its different stages of development including classically known pests (Acraea acerata, Cylas spp.) or as vectors of diseases (Bemisi tabaci, Aphis spp.). The results indicated a high fluctuation in the population density of different pests. The change in the population dynamics were characterized by gradual increase in the populations during rainy seasons followed by decline during dry seasons (hot months of the year). Significant (P<0.05) differences were observed in the population dynamics between sole sweetpotato and mixed sweetpotato intercropping. There was a synchronization of multiple pest generations (biannual, multiannual cycles of reproduction) built up with early rains. The results indicate that rainfall and maximum temperature were critical to the survival and population built up of the pest population. High rainfall in the previous months caused increases in the population density in the subsequent months within a year. The population dynamic (seasonal occurrence) over months and years was likely to coincide with favorable feeding and breeding conditions available within sweetpotato biotopes when temperatures were sufficiently high or after heavy rainfall. For some species, maximum temperature and dry seasons were associated with declines in the pest populations whereas for other species, heavy rainfall was associated with subsequent outbreaks (high populations) in the following months of the years. It is likely that perturbations in temperature/ rainfall patterns may cause serious changes in the pest population, therefore favoring the build-up of multiple generations within a year, thus. Rainfall and maximum temperatures were reliable predictors of key pest species. In fact, regressions analyses indicated that there were significant relationships (P<0.01) between the fluctuation of the population density of different pest species and the variability of climatic factors (mean monthly maximum/ minimum temperature, average rainfall). The population density of different insect pest species varied according to cropping system and to altitude. For example, a significant relationship (P<0.001) was observed between adult aphid population density and average maximum temperature whereas Cylas spp. correlated significantly (P<0.05) with rainfall at high and mid altitudes in both sole and mixed crops. The population density of Acraea acerata was not related to variability in rainfall because the species seemed to occur in number in crops (mono cropping and mixed crops) in marshland areas in June-July and December-February. The virus pressure (measured as the number of leaves symptomatically showing virus attack) followed the population density of whiteflies and aphids. Population trends of other arthropod groups (millipedes, beetles) were not affected by crop variety (clones) or by the altitude or the climate variability but more by the farming practice (mixed or monoculture) implemented by the farmer. It is possible that the resistance or tolerance of some varieties (bio-fortified/vitamin-rich/orange flesh varieties) may be reduced in the future under changing climatic conditions of crop growing in the region with Maximum temperature as the key driver of changes in the population density. The ability to predict the severity of pest populations from mean monthly rainfall/temperature data will provide a significant input into the development of IPM programme for sweetpotato pest species. The data indicates that building resilient sweetpotato crops will require the consideration of various approaches. It is likely that climate change may affect both the pests and vectordiseases and therefore the yield of the crop in eastern DRCongo. Such situation may endanger food security of small scale farmers in the future. Further investigations would be better focus on the understanding on the interacting of climatic, anthropogenic, environmental and soil factors on the pressure of sweetpotato pest in different agro-ecological zones of DRCongo.

title: Crabby Days
abstract: AMONG THE MOST HEAVILY HARVESTED CRUSTACEANS IN THE WORLD IS THE BLUE CRAB, CALLINECTES SAPIDUS, WHOSE SCIENTIFIC NAME TRANSLATES TO (WHAT ELSE?) “SAVORY BEAUTIFUL SWIMMER.” Most people are probably aware that the world’s 70,000 or so species of crustaceans aren’t insects, but folk taxonomy has long recognized a connection. How else to account for whale lice (amphipods), fish lice (branchiurans), woodlice (isopods), sand fleas (hippid decapods and talitrid amphipods), water fleas (cladocerans), pillbugs (isopods), mantis shrimp (stomatopods), and Australia’s Moreton Bay bugs and Balmain bugs (decapods)? To me, though, the resemblance seems remote. Yes, crustaceans have an exoskeleton and jointed appendages, but so do about 100,000 species of arachnids, along with 20,000 or so species of millipedes and centipedes. With respect to legs, the number crustaceans have is wildly inconsistent across groups, and the legs they have are definitely un-entomologically biramous. As for other appurtenances, they have too many antennae (two pairs instead of only one pair), and while there are many conventionally two-eyed crustaceans, others have variously too many (as in the three-eyed notostracan Triops) or not enough (as in the one-eyed copepod Cyclops and the eyeless remipedians in underwater caves). Metamorphosis among these crustaceans looks completely different, too, with some species living planktonic lives as larvae—called variously nauplii, zoeae, or phyllosomas (among others, depending on taxon)—and progressing through a variety of strange taxon-specific stages with no obvious equivalents in insect metamorphosis. That’s why I’ve had so much trouble adjusting to the concept that insects are just terrestrial crustaceans, even though I’ve had 15 years to get used to the idea—ever since molecular phylogenetic studies provided pretty compelling evidence of the relationship (Regier et al. 2005). In addition to their un-insect-like anatomy and development, there’s the fact that cultural attitudes toward insects and crustaceans are poles apart. The key differences appear to be that, first, most people enjoy eating crustaceans; and, second, most people don’t seem to be afraid of most crustaceans. Before writing this column, I had never used the word ostraconophobia, which technically means “fear of shellfish,” a vague term that unites crustaceans and molluscs (in defiance of any molecular evidence), or the word kabourophobia, “fear of crabs and lobsters,” called by one source “an extremely rare phobia” (CAA 2016). If people are afraid of anything related to crabs and lobsters, it’s probably that they might spill some delicious crustacean meat or butter sauce on their clothes (a factor contributing to the invention almost a century ago of the lobster bib). Taxonomically, the name of that new group created by systematists to reflect the relationship between insects and more conventional crustaceans—“Pancrustacea”—even seems like an invitation to cook and consume them. And humans have been doing just that for a very long time. The first archeological evidence of a crustacean-based dinner dates back 125,000 years, at a site on the Red Sea coast of Eritrea, where discovered among the artifacts was an obsidian flake tool, of the sort used to harvest and process food, embedded in the claw of a crab (Walter et al. 2000). I find it odd that there’s a specific term for human consumption of insects (entomophagy) despite the fact that, relatively speaking, the number of English-speaking entomophages is small, yet there is no specific term for eating crustaceans. These long-time menu items are unceremoniously lumped together with molluscs as “shellfish” in the Food and Drug Administration’s Seafood List (FDA 2018) or grouped with “fish” as acceptable fare for pescatarians and the more obscure vegaquarians (some of whom define themselves as eating no meat other than from nonmammalian aquatic animals). We humans are by no means alone in eating crustaceans—in fact, many, if not most, marine organisms find them delicious. For example, krill, members of the order Euphausiacea, are found in all oceans of the world. Generally on the small side, ranging from 8 mm to 6 cm (Tou et al. 2007), krill have locked up the bottom of the animal component of most marine food chains, eating phytoplankton and being eaten by basically everything bigger than they are. The Southern Ocean population of Antarctic krill, Euphausia superba, is estimated to weigh about 380 million tons, more than half of which is consumed by the world’s whales, penguins, seals, squid, fish, and other animals. Humans harvest more modest quantities of krill—around 5.6 million tons per year (CCAMLR 2018). Although much of the harvested krill is used as fish feed, a lot of krill end up crushed, salted, and fermented into shrimp paste, a popular condiment throughout Southeast Asia. As well, sales of krill oil, marketed as a dietary supplement rich in omega-3 fatty acids, are growing by leaps and bounds, bringing in more than $350 million in 2018 (GlobeNewswire 2020). Aside from krill, enormous numbers of crustaceans are fished from the world’s oceans. At the other extreme of marine crustacean size, Macrocheira kaempferi, the Japanese spider crab, has a leg span of up to almost 4 m and a mass of 20 kg, the largest of any arthropod. The first paragraph of the Wikipedia entry for this magnificent creature mentions (unsurprisingly) that it’s “considered a delicacy.” More than 55 species of crabs from 12 different families are harvested for human consumption around the world, amounting to almost two million tons (Stevens and Miller 2020, FAO 2019). Among the most heavily harvested crustaceans in the world is the blue crab, Callinectes sapidus, whose scientific name translates to (what else?) “savory beautiful swimmer.” In 2019, nearly 65 million pounds of blue crabs were harvested from Chesapeake Bay alone (Chesapeake Bay Project 2020). Beyond crabs, the global shrimp catch comprises about 3.4 million tons annually (FAO 2018). IF PEOPLE ARE AFRAID OF ANYTHING RELATED TO CRABS AND LOBSTERS, IT’S PROBABLY THAT THEY MIGHT SPILL SOME DELICIOUS CRUSTACEAN MEAT OR BUTTER SAUCE ON THEIR CLOTHES. Crustaceans aren’t even safe from hungry humans on land. The largest terrestrial arthropod is the coconut crab, Birgus latro, which can weigh up to 9 pounds and live for 60 years. They’re actually endangered in their native Indian and Pacific Oceans because, well, they’re delicious. Nor is there any escape in fresh water: the freshwater crayfish harvest in 2017 amounted to 150 million pounds in the United States alone (Webb 2020). Concerns about crustacean sustainability have led to a massive aquaculture effort and, as a consequence, people harvest and eat almost 8.5 million tons of about 30 species of crustaceans worth more than 60 billion dollars from aquaculture every year, the bulk of which are marine and freshwater shrimp (Tacon 2020). But not all crustaceans can be farmed. Lobsters, for example, present a farming challenge due to their cannibalistic tendencies; evidently, crustaceans are so tasty they even like to eat each other (Romano and Zeng 2017). As a consequence, they’re so valuable that international criminal enterprises have sprung up around acquiring them. For example, this year in Indonesia, the country’s fisheries minister, Edhy Prabowo, reversed a ban on exports that had been enacted by his predecessor, and then proceeded to issue licenses to export larval lobsters to his political cronies, including a company run by a former ministry official who was jailed for lobster smuggling and money laundering (Gokkon 2020). Smugglers have also contributed to global problems with invasive crustaceans. The Chinese mitten crab, Eriocheir sinensis, is native to east Asia but invasive and economically devastating in parts of Europe and North America. A single female can produce up to a million eggs, yielding offspring that clog drainage systems, burrow through dams and levees, and irritate fishermen by damaging nets, stealing bait, eating captured fish out of the nets, and devouring the algae and invertebrates on which fish populations depend. To no one’s surprise, where they’re native, they’re regarded as delicacies, and smugglers catering to mitten crab fans are apprehended with increasing frequency at U.S. ports of entry. Between September 2019 and January 2020, Customs and Border Protection agents confiscated more than 15,000 illegal mitten crabs, with the largest haul—3,700 crabs (3,400 pounds’ worth)—intercepted at the Port of Cincinnati in Erlanger, Kentucky (Latek 2020). Nothing seems to stand in the way of the American appetite for crustaceans. Then came 2020 and the global pandemic. COVID-19 has been an unmitigated disaster for people around the world, but the massive economic disruption caused by the virus has had some unintended benefits for America’s crustaceans. A summer tradition for many coastal communities around the country has been to celebrate crustaceans by boiling them alive and eating enormous quantities of them. A wave of cancellations of crustacean festivals began in March 2020. On 16 March, following a statewide ban on large gatherings by Oregon’s Governor Kate Brown due to the coronavirus pandemic, April’s annual Astoria Warrenton North Coast Crab, Seafood & Wine Festival was cancelled (The Astorian 2020). A month later, the Chamber of Commerce and Visitors Center of Little River in Horry County, South Carolina, announced the postponement of the 39th Annual World Famous Blue Crab Festival in Little River from May until October, when, pandemic permitting, it will be combined with the Little River Shrimpfest (Blondin 2020). On 5 June, the Annual Dungeness Crab & Seafood Festival, which typically brings crowds of 20,000 people to Port Angeles, Washington, in October, was cancelled, sparing the lives (based on last year’s figures) of about 18,000 pounds’ worth of crabs (Carman 2020). Other crab festivals either cancelled, postponed, or converted to online versions include Alaska’s Kodiak Crab Fest, Maryland’s J. Millard Tawes Crab and Clam Bake in Crisfield, and Florida’s Palatka Blue Crab Festival. Those are just the crab festivals quashed by the coronavirus pandemic. Lobster festivals were cancelled in Rockland, Maine (the Maine Lobster Festival), Winter Harbor, Maine (the Winter Harbor Lobster Festival), and Fontana, Wisconsin (the Big Foot Lions Club Lobster Boil & Steak Fry). Cancelled shrimp festivals include Alabama’s National Shrimp Festival in Gulf Shores and both the annual Fernandina Beach Shrimp Fest and the Fort Myers Beach Lions Club Shrimp Festival in Florida. The Rotary Shrimp Fest of South Texas (in downtown Harlingen) has been optimistically rescheduled for mid-September. There’s one marine arthropod, though, that gets no COVID-19 relief—in fact, the virus may have put a target on its carapace. Because the copper-rich blood of the Atlantic horseshoe crab, Limulus polyphemus, coagulates in the presence of endotoxin polysaccharides from Gram-negative bacteria, these arthropods have been gathered, bled, and released back to beaches for decades in order to prepare an extract—Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL)—for use in testing vaccines for microbial contamination. This procedure is understandably hard on the horseshoe crabs, a significant proportion of which don’t survive the blood donation, so developing a synthetic alternative has been a priority. This year, the U.S. Pharmacopeia, which provides guidelines for the pharmaceutical industry, evaluated the synthetic substitute recombinant Factor C (rFC), developed by the Swiss company Lonza, for approval. However, it ultimately declined to approve the synthetic substitute outright over concerns about the safety of new vaccines, many (millions) of which will, in theory, imminently need testing for efficacy against COVID-19. Of course, name notwithstanding, horseshoe crabs have nothing to do with crustaceans, edible or otherwise. They’re arachnids, more closely related to crab spiders than to spider crabs. That fact, however, has proved to be too subtle for many news outlets, which have left the horseshoes out of their headlines for stories on the USP decision. Reuters reported that “Drug Standards Group Nixes Plan to Kick Pharma’s Crab Blood Habit” (Miller 2020); NJ Spotlight ran a story with the headline “Big Pharma Urged to Drop Crab-Blood Test for Possible Covid-19 Vaccine” (Hurdle 2020); Popular Mechanics called its story “Crab Blood Can Save Your Life, but Not the Synthetic Stuff” (Delbert 2020); the BBC asked, “Why Are We ‘Milking’ Crabs for a Coronavirus Vaccine?” (BBC News 2020); and Euronews reported that “Crab Blood Used to Make Covid-19 Vaccine Outrages Animal Rights Activists” (de Ferrer 2020). Okay, outrage is rightly focused on avoidable exploitation of a critically threatened species and not on a taxonomic faux pas, but I think entomologists are entitled to be at least a little indignant that, by dropping one word, news outlets cavalierly converted an arachnid into a crustacean. That said, classifying insects as terrestrial crustaceans puts Pthirus pubis in an entirely new light for me. Given that its official common name is “crab louse” (due to its crablike tarsal claws and body shape), does that mean there are now two groups of terrestrial crustaceans that can legitimately be called crabs? Fortunately, although the creation of Pancrustacea sent entomologists rewriting textbooks, my favorite louse-related joke remains timeless. I’m sure you know it—it’s the one that starts with the question “Why does the ocean roar?” and ends with “You would, too, if you had crabs on your bottom.” Feel free to bring it to a Crab Festival near you when they start back up again next year.

title: Inspiration in Unexpected Ways
abstract: Illinois Insects and Spiders . Macnamara, P. ( paintings ). Text by Division of Insects at the Field Museum . The University of Chicago Press , Chicago , IL . 124 pp. 28 color plates . $16.00 (paperback) . ISBN 0-226-50100-0 . First, you will reach for this book because of the gorgeous art. Then you will admire the delicate design and typography. But this beautiful, small volume, which starts as a tabletop gift book, will end up being one of your favorite field guides. Why? Because there are two sorts of treasure here. The first treasure is Peggy Macnamara's beautiful watercolors; the next is the witty, astonishing, and erudite text created by the Division of Insects at Chicago's Field Museum. Bugs can be a hard sell, but this book is brimming with such artistic and pedagogical joy for its topic that it will capture diverse readers. This is an everyman, three-generation book that could well begin a life-long love of amateur—or even professional—entomology. Peggy Macnamara is artist-in-residence and an associate in the Zoology Department at the Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago, and associate professor at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. For 25 years she has been painting from the museum's collections, providing in-museum demonstrations, and has taught natural-science art extensively. Visitors to the Field Museum have the opportunity to watch her paint and then to observe finished paintings mounted next to dioramas of the charismatic animals depicted in the artworks. Macnamara shares with the public the gift of the great animal painters—in the stillness of a painting, she can express the essence of movement particular to that species. One can almost hear her zebras snort and stamp. In previously published posters and books Macnamara's passionate love of the animals' forms and movements, personalities, and habitats are exquisitely rendered in energetic, expert watercolors. No doubt the triumph of those previous works inspired this latest project with the Field Museum's entomologists. Traditionally, the scientific illustration of Arthropoda generally falls to more precise techniques such as stippled ink drawings or digital illustration. Can this accomplished artist grapple successfully with such different anatomies … and biomechanics? It seems almost logical that watercolors might not capture the clockwork progress of a foraging millipede. This is an artist who deeply connects with the life force of her subjects—why did the Field Museum assign dead bugs on pins? One senses her palpable wish for living subjects in her comments about Plate XVII: Drawing of a Living Mantid. “Having drawn pinned, lifeless insects for years, I found this to be a very rewarding experience. The mantid seems to be staring at me. I came to look forward to its particular gaze each morning.” One can hardly guess what sensitive portraits Macnamara might have painted in a live insect zoo. Better yet, perhaps the Field Museum could commission Macnamara to create a few heroic insect portraits, invoking the fierce energy of Sue—her painting of the Field Museum's iconic T. rex fossil. Macnamara is a scientific illustrator, yes, but she is definitely capable of creating creature imagery that could turn the head of a Hollywood art director. Macnamara has countered this assignment's conundrum by creating exquisitely designed groupings of insects. Her mannered layouts are satisfyingly Victorian, and a certain elegant stillness haunts the plates, as if they are a painted citrine. Macnamara documents the moods of her artistic journey from Chordata to Arthropoda in her fascinating introduction. She speaks of how the traditional naturalist's curiosity pushed her through her reticence. She says, “I became uneasy when I learned that I would need to use a microscope … . My worries were quickly replaced by excitement. Amazed by its body's outrageous colors and patterns, I felt lost, silly in love. I began drawing forms I had never seen before, gradually forgetting my old methods and creating new ones.” Ms. Macnamara's comments link the method of scientific observation and art demonstrably and inextricably. Macnamara writes “Insects as ‘artist-actors’ soon fascinated me. By impersonating the habitats around them, they literally draw their surroundings on themselves in order to blend in. Moths become leaves, beetles become bark, and false eyes are everywhere. Their reflective surfaces distort form and help them disappear. They appear light where a shadow would otherwise make them dark and obviously round. As if using good drawing practices, insects dissolve their form rather than make it obvious … .” Macnamara's camouflaged mastery is evident as she creates the mood of casual field observation that is missing in other insect guides. But do not be fooled—the backyard scientist will not be disappointed. The facts, identification keys, and telltale details are precisely painted. The entomologist authors, too, are well attuned to providing rigorous visual identification. Their text clearly shows that artists and scientists share the same precise observational skills. Expertise overlap when the text states that monarch butterflies may actually be mimicking viceroys, and that hairstreak butterflies can be identified by the band of white scales around their eyes. The collaboration between the artist and the scientists is clearly evident throughout the book, as if their offices are, yes, indeed, just down the hall. Artists of all stripes will enjoy the mastery of the paintings in Illinois Insects and Spiders, such as the stunning Plate XI Dog Day Cicada. The Plates XIV and XV Moths I and Moths II, respectively, have gorgeous, sensitive uses of the color complements blue-greens and magentas, with pigments rejected by some artists as garish and by some printers as irreproducible. She adds this insight to her introduction: “I was also forced to change my palette to accommodate insects. I needed to use more fluorescent and bright colors as well as earth tones made up of layered opposites and metallics. Later, when I took the revised palette outside, my landscapes improved … .” Notoriously difficult, the dark but iridescent colors of the mourning cloak butterfly and red-spotted purple are handsomely painted in Plate XVI Common Butterflies. In Plate XVII Swallowtails we are given, at last, some gyrating caterpillars. We are also given the undermarkings of the butterflies, which are not really necessary for identification. One feels Macnamara's relief at painting subjects for which she has more affinity. Was it a missed opportunity not to paint the spectacular silk moths and their caterpillars, which could showcase Macnamara's eloquence with creature movement? For capturing that astonishing, otherworldly athleticism of insects one need only turn a field lens onto the educational text. These comments should not be neglected because they are small. Both levels of Illinois Insect and Spiders—text and art—will reward even the briefest glance. Easy entry points into the anthropology and science of insects are present and abundant in the notes of every beautiful plate. The everyday science of the text, which benefits significantly from the voice of one particularly joyous entomologist, abounds with infectious wonder: “When scaled to human proportions, the ambush of some species (of tiger beetles) is equivalent to more than 300 miles per hour!” More athletic marvels reward the imaginations of the readers. The oak gall wasps can catapult the little balls in which they live; bluet (darners) females can spend up to an hour underwater while laying eggs; and ebony jewelwings (damselflies) can snap their wings to indicate their locations to their mates, who engage in lethal dogfights for love. The editors have carefully selected common insects that are divas or rogues in their unique way and have brought their characters into sharp focus with spare, engaging, and educational descriptions. Additionally, “gee-whiz” notes from all the natural sciences shine through the text from the fields of botany, geology, paleontology, and ecological restoration. The authors and editors must be proud of sumptuous sentences such as: “This metallic, gem-like ‘green-eyed dragon’ lives only in spring-fed marshes and sedge meadows high in calcium carbonate based on a substrate of dolomite bedrock.” One of the continuing threads is the links and comparisons between living and fossil insects. How wondrous it is to read about a 200-year-old glacial deposit of a locust swarm—a locust species that is now extinct. All ages will delight to the tone of the writing, which purposefully veers the reader between the horror and glee that is natural for humans considering the habits of insects. Prairie ecology and restoration is a continuing topic in Illinois Insect and Spiders. The Field Museum supports education, research, and prairie conservation projects as part of their outreach work. This reviewer appreciated the efforts by these museum authors to bring prairie awareness to this book. Reports of conservation efforts—successful and awry—are mentioned throughout the text, including Chicago's history with the notorious Asian longhorn beetle. Typical of the scope of the text, it ranges from a child's backlot screamer (giant, but harmless, yellow and black spiders) to the specialists' rare find (clouded crimson moth) as barometers of true prairie health. The authors report, with regrets, the story of the Karner blue butterfly, lupines, and their unsuccessful introduction into Lake Superior dunes in Zion, Illinois. Simple advice is also available, such as the fact that the Missouri goldenrod retreats into a 13-year dormancy when eaten clean by its beetle. The authors underscore that ecology is essential to everyone by including tips for gardeners. One of the notes mentions that mail-order ladybugs are supposed to fly away from the garden you bought them for because they are genetically scripted to do so. The reader learns that they gather by the thousands to rest on shiny buildings in the fall, and are an introduction to the United States that is threatening the displacement of our native species. This gardener just nodded knowingly when the text described the horrible smell from a black swallowtail caterpillar, which this book says is emitted from glands inside their heads which, when threatened, turn inside out like antlers. Believe me, it is an unforgettable, stinky entomological feat. Anyone would race to a field guide to identify this. Perhaps Illinois Insect and Spiders will motivate you to take a child, microphone, and laptop out to the garden to record the buffalo leafhopper. Or, even more likely, to draw and paint their amazing stripes and colors. With a hand lens, this book will inspire you in unexpected ways. It belongs in the libraries of artists and naturalists all over the country, not just in Illinois. Peggy Macnamara says, “I have found that the insect experience is a prescription for life. I see the value in moving a little slower, looking ever more closely, and finding treasures in the seemingly mundane. Each local population is worth study and admiration, and where I am is where to begin.” Fine and wise counsel from a fine and wise little guide.
